item.title: Recomendaciones del Festival de cine de San Sebastián
item.description: El Festival de Cine de San Sebastián tiene algo de maratón: durante nueve días, películas, nombres e historias se suceden a un ritmo que hace imposible verlo todo. Pero entre lo que he podido ver en esta edición hay tres películas muy diferentes que se han quedado conmigo. Una revisita a Thomas Mann en su regreso a la Alemania de posguerra; otra se adentra en el Nueva York artístico y gay de los años 1980 en plena crisis del sida; y la tercera encuentra, en el universo underground neoyorquino, una historia inesperadamente tierna sobre crecer. Son Fatherland, The Man I Love y Club Kid: tres películas que recomiendo buscar cuando continúen su recorrido después del festival.

item.title: Election integrity and voting rights are not opposing principles
item.description:
When I served as a state trooper, enforcing the law and protecting people’s constitutional rights were never competing responsibilities.

They were the job.

That same principle should guide the person South Dakota entrusts with administering our elections.

Our state constitution begins its article on elections with remarkably clear language: “Elections shall be free and equal.” It says no civil or military power may interfere with the free exercise of the right to vote. It also says that every U.S. citizen 18 or older who meets our residency and registration requirements is entitled to vote, while giving the Legislature authority to establish reasonable requirements to ensure the integrity of the vote.

Those principles do not contradict each other.

We can protect the integrity of our elections and protect the rights of eligible voters. In fact, we have to do both.

A dispute unfolding in South Dakota this year shows why that distinction matters.

During the 2026 legislative session, lawmakers passed Senate Bill 175, which requires documentary proof of citizenship from new voter registration applicants. Without the required documentation, an applicant can be registered as a “federal-only” voter, able to vote in federal contests but not state or local elections.

There is a legitimate public discussion to have about that policy. But there is another question that matters just as much to the Secretary of State: What happens after a law is passed?

The League of Women Voters of South Dakota petitioned the State Board of Elections for changes to how the new requirement was administered. Among the issues it raised were how certain documents could be submitted and what happened when a voter was placed into federal-only status.

The Board ultimately rejected the petition on a procedural issue. South Dakota Searchlightreported on that July 8 decision.

Heather Baxter, now the Republican nominee for Secretary of State and a supporter of SB 175 during the legislative session, submitted written comments opposing the League’s proposals. She characterized them as “a way for the League to abolish SB175” and argued against allowing photocopies of certain identification documents.

But that was not the end of the issue.

On Aug. 24, the League and Sioux Falls resident Jaysen Hill filed a federal lawsuit against Secretary of State Monae Johnson and members of the State Board of Elections. Importantly, the plaintiffs do not ask the court to eliminate South Dakota’s documentary proof-of-citizenship requirement. Their claims challenge aspects of how the state has implemented it. The plaintiffs allege, among other things, that some federal-only voters were not accurately informed why their registrations had been restricted or how to correct the problem. Read the federal complaint and case materials.

Hill’s experience illustrates why administration matters.

According to the lawsuit, he mailed his registration with a photocopy of his South Dakota identification card and was classified as a federal-only voter. But the notice he received said the problem involved his residential address, even though he had supplied one. He alleges he did not learn what he actually needed to correct in time to vote in state and local contests in the June primary. Those remain allegations in ongoing litigation, not final findings by a court.

Then something important happened.

After the lawsuit was filed and a federal judge heard arguments, Secretary Johnson issued new guidance to county auditors. Her office provided separate notice letters for different reasons a voter might receive federal-only status, directed auditors to stop sending inaccurate notices, and instructed them to send corrected information to affected voters so they would have an opportunity to restore full-voter status before the registration deadline. South Dakota Searchlight reported on those changes Sept. 15.

Three days later, U.S. District Judge Eric Schulte denied the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction as moot. His reason is important: the Secretary of State had made the changes requested in that motion and had committed not to return to the prior practice. The order did not resolve every issue in the broader lawsuit, which remains active. Read Judge Schulte’s Sept. 18 order.

To me, there is a lesson here that is larger than one bill, one lawsuit or one election. Passing an election law is one thing. Administering it fairly and competently is another.

The Secretary of State is not simply an advocate for election legislation. The office has to turn laws into forms, instructions, computer systems, deadlines and procedures that county auditors can actually administer and South Dakotans can actually understand.

When a problem emerges, the question should not begin with which political side raised it. The question should be: Is there a problem, and what does the law require us to do about it?

My background in law enforcement shaped how I think about that responsibility. A law enforcement officer has authority, but that authority exists within a constitutional framework. You enforce the law, follow the facts, and respect due process. You are responsible for protecting the rights of the people you serve.

Election administration deserves the same discipline.

If someone is not legally eligible to vote, our election laws should prevent an unlawful ballot from being cast. But when a South Dakotan is legally entitled to vote, our government should administer those laws accurately enough that the voter knows what is required and has a fair opportunity to exercise that right.

That should not be a partisan proposition.

Election integrity does not require us to choose between enforcing the rules and protecting voting rights. Good election administration requires both. Election integrity does not require us to choose between enforcing the rules and protecting voting rights. Good election administration requires both.

Terrence Davis is the Democratic candidate for South Dakota Secretary of State. A Sioux Falls resident, husband and father, Davis previously served as a state trooper in Tennessee and with the South Dakota Highway Patrol and later worked with East River Legal Services. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Criminal Justice and a master’s degree in Public Policy and is pursuing a doctoral degree in Law and Policy. This is his first campaign for elected office.

item.title: Finding common ground in the U.S.-China AI rivalry
item.description:
AI is the big item on the agenda this week as Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with President Trump in Washington, D.C.


The talks come after a firestorm of news that has brought AI safety front and center: the hack of Hugging Face by rogue OpenAI agents, the resignation of an Anthropic researcher, plus calls by AI leaders to pace the frontier always met with the rejoinder, “what about China?”


Samm Sacks, senior fellow at the think tank New America, tells us more about China's approach to these AI talks.


More on this:


“US and China Hail Talks as Positive Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit” from Bloomberg


“US proposes AI incident alert system in talks with China, Bessent says” from Associated Press

item.title: John Thune is posting fantasy these days. Says Trump keeps his promises
item.description:
In a dutifully ingratiating piece that’s sure to meet with President Trump’s approval, our senior senator John Thune a few days ago posted a string of predictably flattering observations about Trump in his weekly column, titled “Promises made, promises kept.”

Thune’s missive is off, way off, and reflects the fact that Trump supporters are living in a political fantasyland.

  • Thune starts by noting that two years ago “our country was dealing with an inflation crisis.” That’s a gross exaggeration. In December 2024, U.S. inflation stood at 2.9%. That was just about the average inflation rate for the ten years prior, and nearly a full percent lower than the 3.77% average inflation rate for the 50 years prior. Thune’s claim that Trump inherited an inflation “crisis” is not only baloney, its implication that Trump, whose vow to do something about it on day one was a promise made and kept is spectacularly wrong. Inflation has worsened under Trump. Inflation over the last 12 months was 3.4%. 

  • Thune also notes that the country was facing an “historic immigration crisis” when Trump took office in 2025. Trump promised to do something about it, but I don’t get where things have improved on the immigration front since Trump took over. Illegal crossings are down, but the larger humanitarian crisis that caused them in the first place still exists, shaming our country’s indifference to it. Meantime, Trump’s hard line policies toward removing undocumented aliens have backfired to the point where most Americans dislike them. Inhumane tactics and conditions are widely reported, and there have been economic consequences. Labor shortages around the country have been cropping up, a situation that the Trump administration has ignored. On a local note, the Economic Policy Institute says that if Trump achieves its deportation targets, 6,000 jobs will be lost in South Dakota. Thune thinks this is praiseworthy? Please.

  • Thune rejoices that Americans got a tax cut this year from Trump’s “Working Families Tax Cut.” The Treasury Dept. calculates that families saved $1300-$1700 a year on taxes in 2026, which only tells part of the story. According to the congressional Joint Economic Committee - Minority, Trump’s tariffs, actually a tax because Americans pay them, cost American families about $1700 each in 2025, effectively canceling out the tax cut’s savings.

  • Then after this litany of misinformation, Thune concludes: “Our work is not done.”

  • To which I repeat a friend’s mantra: SO MUCH WINNING!! Stop it, Donnie. I can’t take it anymore.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.title: The beauty industry is betting big on AI
item.description:
The global beauty market is expected to hit almost $600 billion by 2030, according to a report by McKinsey & Company. And just like pretty much every industry, it's being transformed by AI.


L’Oréal and OpenAI announced a partnership this summer to bring virtual makeup try-ons and product discovery to ChatGPT. An AI styling firm called Alta is integrating e.l.f. Beauty products into its virtual try on avatars. And consumers are increasingly looking to chatbots for skincare and makeup recommendations.


Apparently beauty inquiries account for almost half of generative AI retail referral traffic, according to market research firm EuroMonitor. For more we're joined by fashion-tech journalist and consultant Maghan McDowell, who's been following this trend.
item.source:markdown:
The global beauty market is expected to hit almost $600 billion by 2030, [according to a report by McKinsey & Company](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/consumer-packaged-goods/our-insights/state-of-beauty). And just like pretty much every industry, it's being transformed by AI.
L’Oréal and OpenAI [announced](https://www.loreal.com/en/press-release/research-and-innovation/l-oreal-and-openai-join-forces-for-transformation-in-beauty-with-ai/) a partnership this summer to bring virtual makeup try-ons and product discovery to ChatGPT. An AI styling firm called Alta [is integrating e.l.f. Beauty products into its virtual try on avatars](https://www.vogue.com/article/why-elf-beauty-is-building-avatars-with-ai-platform-alta). And consumers are increasingly looking to chatbots for skincare and makeup recommendations.
Apparently beauty inquiries account for almost half of generative AI retail referral traffic, according to [market research firm EuroMonitor](https://www.euromonitor.com/article/genai-discovery-and-the-changing-shopper-funnel). For more we're joined by fashion-tech journalist and consultant [Maghan McDowell](https://www.maghanmcdowell.com/), who's been following this trend.

item.title: Any scholarship or financial reward comes at a price
item.description:
A full ride academic or athletic scholarship is the gold standard for college funding, an unrealistic dream for many families and an achievement to celebrate for a few. A recent conversation with one of those scholarship recipients gave me a new perspective on that dream.

At age twelve, Jaelyn Vickery was playing travel softball in front of college recruiters, flying around the country most weekends with a team that met to compete and never practiced together. By fifteen she had committed to playing in the Big Ten on a scholarship that would cover her tuition, housing, and books. She graduated from the University of Illinois with two degrees and no student loans, the outcome most families hope for.

Now, as a young adult, Jaelyn is establishing herself in a career she loves—not as an athlete or a coach, but as a financial therapist. Part of the reason for the shift is the price she paid for her “free” education. Like every financial reward, it came with a cost.

When I asked Jae what her cost had been, she did not have to think about it. She said identity. She gave up family vacations, school dances, friends' birthday parties, and the ordinary preteen and teen years when most of us begin to find out who we are with nobody keeping score. In return she got a large financial number attached to her name. Her net worth and her self-worth fused before she was old enough to drive.

By her senior year in college Jae had the accolades and the grades, and she told me she was performing at a level she could not feel. She described it as several years of doing everything right while being somewhere else the whole time. Her department offered her a medical redshirt for mental health that kept her financial aid in place without requiring her to compete. Taking it meant walking away from the final season of something she had built since she was ten. She took it.

That year she managed her own money for the first time. A job at a bank then started her on a path that led her to the field of financial therapy.

Listening to Jae’s story, I kept thinking about the Olympic gymnasts and swimmers we watch every four years, fifteen and sixteen years old on a world stage, and what it costs to be that good that early. The obvious price includes the investment of time from both the young athlete and the parents as well as the financial cost of lessons, equipment, and travel. The unseen price is the emotional toll for everyone. This has many possible forms, such as the burden for the athlete of carrying their own and others’ expectations, the resentment of siblings whose needs and dreams may slip to second place, or the struggle for parents to juggle the additional load of the athletic activity as well as the ordinary complications of family life.

My intent is not to discourage students and their families from going after scholarships or aspiring to reach elite levels in athletics or in music, drama, and other arts. For those with the skills and passion, it may be exactly the right path.

What I strongly recommend is to pay attention to the emotional and financial costs as well as the possibilities. This is true for any financial goal or reward: a scholarship, a lucrative career, a job title, or a milestone net worth number. Each one carries a price. If that price starts to outweigh the reward, as it did for Jae, it may be time to consider shifting toward a different path.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

item.source:markdown:
A full ride academic or athletic scholarship is the gold standard for college funding, an unrealistic dream for many families and an achievement to celebrate for a few. A recent conversation with one of those scholarship recipients gave me a new perspective on that dream.
At age twelve, [Jaelyn Vickery](https://us.list-manage.com/Mu3NpS2Tcyq?e=f6092c9c7b&c2id=bb5d24e9334e337e2f8dc8f2d6061031) was playing travel softball in front of college recruiters, flying around the country most weekends with a team that met to compete and never practiced together. By fifteen she had committed to playing in the Big Ten on a scholarship that would cover her tuition, housing, and books. She graduated from the University of Illinois with two degrees and no student loans, the outcome most families hope for.
Now, as a young adult, Jaelyn is establishing herself in a career she loves—not as an athlete or a coach, but as a financial therapist. Part of the reason for the shift is the price she paid for her “free” education. Like every financial reward, it came with a cost.
When I asked Jae what her cost had been, she did not have to think about it. She said identity. She gave up family vacations, school dances, friends' birthday parties, and the ordinary preteen and teen years when most of us begin to find out who we are with nobody keeping score. In return she got a large financial number attached to her name. Her net worth and her self-worth fused before she was old enough to drive.
By her senior year in college Jae had the accolades and the grades, and she told me she was performing at a level she could not feel. She described it as several years of doing everything right while being somewhere else the whole time. Her department offered her a medical redshirt for mental health that kept her financial aid in place without requiring her to compete. Taking it meant walking away from the final season of something she had built since she was ten. She took it.
That year she managed her own money for the first time. A job at a bank then started her on a path that led her to the field of financial therapy.
Listening to Jae’s story, I kept thinking about the Olympic gymnasts and swimmers we watch every four years, fifteen and sixteen years old on a world stage, and what it costs to be that good that early. The obvious price includes the investment of time from both the young athlete and the parents as well as the financial cost of lessons, equipment, and travel. The unseen price is the emotional toll for everyone. This has many possible forms, such as the burden for the athlete of carrying their own and others’ expectations, the resentment of siblings whose needs and dreams may slip to second place, or the struggle for parents to juggle the additional load of the athletic activity as well as the ordinary complications of family life.
My intent is not to discourage students and their families from going after scholarships or aspiring to reach elite levels in athletics or in music, drama, and other arts. For those with the skills and passion, it may be exactly the right path.
What I strongly recommend is to pay attention to the emotional and financial costs as well as the possibilities. This is true for any financial goal or reward: a scholarship, a lucrative career, a job title, or a milestone net worth number. Each one carries a price. If that price starts to outweigh the reward, as it did for Jae, it may be time to consider shifting toward a different path.
_Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge._

item.title: The cost of digitally disconnecting
item.description:
Sure, you can put down your phone and go touch grass for free. But for those looking for a little help committing to a more disconnected lifestyle, there's a growing market of products and services from retreats to apps to devices that promise to supercharge your ability to unplug — for a price. Paula Mejia has covered the booming digital detox industry for Mother Jones, and spoke with “Marketplace Tech” host Meghan McCarty Carino about her reporting.


More on this:

item.title: More: Medicaid expansion and constitutional amendment I
item.description:
I recently posted my view that constitutional amendment I on November’s ballot would jeopardize Medicaid expansion in South Dakota, then posted a note I got from Lt. Governor Tony Venhuizen as an addendum to my piece.

The amendment’s passage would give South Dakota’s government the ability to change or altogether eliminate Medicaid expansion if the federal government’s part of the financing falls below 90% of the program’s cost.

As to the ‘change’ part, Venhuizen’s note said that if the constitutional amendment passed, it would not automatically trigger an elimination of Medicaid expansion. 

As to the ‘eliminate’ part, based on Attorney General Jackley’s interpretation of the measure, Venhuizen is wrong.  Per Jackley, in his explanation statement to Secretary of State Johnson last May, “This proposed Constitutional Amendment ends the expanded Medicaid coverage if the federal funding for expansion drops below 90%.”

Jackley’s interpretation seems clear and unequivocal to me, but if my interpretation is wrong and Venhuizen’s explanation is right, we’d have a scenario that would make Medicaid expansion the political football it had been for many years. South Dakotans, fed up by legislative foot-dragging, forced its implementation by voting it in via a constitutional amendment in November 2022. Republican leaders, including then-Gov. Kristi Noem, called the measure fiscally irresponsible, but a majority, 56%, of South Dakota voters disagreed and voted to extend Medicaid coverage to about 30,000 people who earn too much to qualify for Medicaid but not enough to pay for private health insurance.

With the federal government covering 90% of the cost of Medicaid expansion, South Dakota’s cost is somewhere between $35-$40 million annually.

What started this year’s movement to remove Medicaid expansion from our state’s constitution was some budgetary cost reductions that were considered last spring by the Trump administration. Though the federal government’s 90% share of costs remains intact, the chance that it may be reduced is in the minds of state legislators, so much so that 14 states have automatic “trigger” laws calling for elimination or reconsideration of Medicaid expansion if the federal government’s share of the cost falls below 90%.

Passage of constitutional amendment I would add South Dakota to that list, being among the states, if Jackley’s interpretation is right, that would eliminate Medicaid expansion altogether. 

I oppose the possibility of that happening. 

Missing from the view of supporters of this harsh scenario is some consideration for the 30,000 South Dakotans who depend on Medicaid expansion.  

Everyone appreciates that South Dakota’s legislators need to take a hard look at every penny of state support for Medicaid expansion, but that should be done in the overall context of what happens, not just to human beings, but to the general economy when spending cuts are implemented or programs disappear altogether.  

The Rural Hospital Association is unequivocal about the gains received by rural health care providers through Medicaid coverage. All, not just rural, hospitals will be significantly affected because uncompensated care costs will increase. The only way those losses can be recovered is by increasing costs to the general population. 

On a broad level, The American Medical Association reminds us that a healthy population is a major driver of a strong economy.

South Dakota’s tight labor market needs all the healthy job applicants it can get.  

Our cost-conscious state legislature should take a “big picture” perspective on the matter and commit itself to finding ways of making up for the possibility of reduced federal spending on Medicaid. In a state that routinely has significant budget surpluses, we can be humane and fiscally responsible simultaneously.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Kristi Noem, called the measure fiscally irresponsible, but a majority, 56%, of South Dakota voters disagreed and voted to extend Medicaid coverage to about 30,000 people who earn too much to qualify for Medicaid but not enough to pay for private health insurance.

What started this year’s movement to remove Medicaid expansion from our state’s constitution was some budgetary cost reductions that were [considered last spring](https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/trump-administration-proposes-cracking-down-medicaid-state-directed-payments/820794/) by the Trump administration. Though the federal government’s 90% share of costs remains intact, the chance that it may be reduced is in the minds of state legislators, so much so that [14 states](https://www.healthinsurance.org/faqs/which-states-have-trigger-laws-to-automatically-end-medicaid-expansion-if-federal-funding-drops/) have automatic “trigger” laws calling for elimination or reconsideration of Medicaid expansion if the federal government’s share of the cost falls below 90%.
Passage of constitutional amendment I would add South Dakota to that list, being among the states, if Jackley’s interpretation is right, that would eliminate Medicaid expansion altogether.
I oppose the possibility of that happening.
Missing from the view of supporters of this harsh scenario is some consideration for the 30,000 South Dakotans who depend on Medicaid expansion.
Everyone appreciates that South Dakota’s legislators need to take a hard look at every penny of state support for Medicaid expansion, but that should be done in the overall context of what happens, not just to human beings, but to the general economy when spending cuts are implemented or programs disappear altogether.
The [Rural Hospital Association](https://www.aha.org/fact-sheets/2026-03-02-medicaid-coverage-supports-rural-patients-hospitals-and-communities) is unequivocal about the gains received by rural health care providers through Medicaid coverage. All, not just rural, hospitals [will be significantly affected](https://www.rwjf.org/en/insights/our-research/2025/03/hospital-revenue-losses-and-increased-uncompensated-care-if-medicaid-funding-is-cut.html) because uncompensated care costs will increase. The only way those losses can be recovered is by increasing costs to the general population.
On a broad level, The American Medical Association reminds us that a [healthy population](https://www.ama-assn.org/public-health/optimal-health/healthy-population-equals-healthy-economy) is a major driver of a strong economy.

item.title: How attitudes toward AI differ across generations
item.description:
At this point we've probably all been a part of heated dinner conversations about AI. Rana el Kaliouby has them almost nightly at home. She's an AI scientist and investor who hosts the podcast Pioneers of AI.

item.title: Constitutional amendment J is about who controls elections
item.description:
John’s note: the is the second of a series on the constitutional amendments that will be on our ballots in November. Amendment J is a blanket ban on non-citizens voting in state and local elections in South Dakota.

First off, under current state law, I think constitutional amendment J is probably unnecessary in South Dakota. On a federal level, non-citizens, since the 1920s, have already been barred from voting in federal elections. Amendment J codifies and extends that denial to South Dakota state and local elections. But, since U.S. citizenship is already required to register to vote in this state, I don’t get why we need a constitutional amendment that is essentially redundant.  

My beef with this amendment is that it takes local decision-making away from localities that  want to make their own decisions about who gets to vote in their elections. There are jurisdictions around the United States that allow non-citizens who reside here legally to vote in local elections, probably on the basis that many of these people live, work, pay taxes, and generally participate in local life alongside American citizens.They’re stakeholders and taxpayers in their communities and it seems reasonable that they should be able to have their say in local elections.

I think local communities should have the option of deciding who can vote in their elections. I don’t want to see a constitutional amendment that denies localities the chance to make that decision. 

I’m voting no on constitutional amendment J.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.title: Constitutional amendment I jeopardizes Medicaid expansion.
item.description:
John’s note: I added Lieutenant Governor Tony Venhuizen’s comment on this piece to the end of my column. I invite readers to review it as an additional consideration as to how constituional amendment I would affect Medicaid expaonsion if it passes.

Constitutional amendment I would yank Medicaid eligibility for some 30,000 South Dakotans if the federal commitment to fund 90% of the cost of Medicaid expansion were to cease or be reduced.  I get that Medicaid expansion passed by a vote in 2022, when it was clear that the feds would pay for 90% of it. If for some reason that promise changes and drops to a level below 90%, constitutional amendment I would end the program.

This seems harsh to me.

A peremptory denial of health care to people desperately in need of it based on a change in the funding formula is inhumane. We South Dakotans can do better, particularly in a state that consistently brags about its budget surpluses. 2026 marked 15 consecutive years during which our state has had a budget surplus.

Finding a way to use that excess cash for poor people who need health care seems like the right thing to do.  

Vote no on this harsh and uncharitable dismissal of needy people.

Lt. Governor Venhuizen’s response to the above: Amendment I is not an automatic trigger. SD's participation in Medicaid Expansion is required by our State Medicaid Plan, which is an agreement between the state (Dept. of Social Services) and the feds, and participation in expansion is also built into the state budget.

If Amendment I were to pass, and then at some future point the feds backed down from their 90% match (as they very nearly did in 2025 in the One Big Beautiful Bill), the effect of Amendment I would be to remove the constitutional requirement that the state participate. But it would not preclude the state from continuing to participate. And continuing to participate would be the default, because expansion would continue to be part of the State Medicaid Plan.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.       

Photo: public domain, wikimedia commons 

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

item.title: Trump rejects AI's "effective altruism" movement
item.description:
Congress is looking to rein in Flock cameras; plus, Apple has a new way to prove your iPhone photos are real.


But first, it's been a wild week in AI. After the freakout over an Anthropic researcher quitting in protest last week, CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in AI, and his counterpoints Sam Altman and Elon Musk agreed. President Donald Trump? Not so much. He called fears of rogue AI a hoax, and even went after a niche intellectual community that's deeply invested in AI safety: the Effective Altruist movement.


Paresh Dave, senior writer at Wired, joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino to explain more about all this on this week’s “Tech Bytes: Week in Review.”


Check out our YouTube page to watch more episodes of “Tech Bytes.”

item.title: Fed raises interest rates, exposes Trump’s ineptitude
item.description:
As if we needed more verification of President Trump’s inability to control the world and make it spin to his liking, the Federal Reserve Board just announced that interest rates are going up. Why? Because inflation is still unacceptably high.

Trump, who vowed that grocery prices would come down on “day one” of his administration and that he would get inflation under control, has been exposed as a victim of his own ineptitude.

  • Despite warning after warning that his tariff fixation would raise prices on nearly everything that Americans buy, Trump went ahead with his plans to tariff just about every country in sight. The result? Tariffs drove excess inflation.

  • Despite his promise that the war with Iran would be over in a few weeks, Trump found out he grabbed a tiger by its tail. Here we are, eight months into a war that looks like it has no end in sight, dealing with some of the highest energy prices ever because of it.

  • Despite blaming high prices on the Biden administration, inflation has accelerated since Trump took office in 2025.

These facts, as you might expect, haven’t done much to bring Trump back into contact with reality.  He’s still delusionally claiming that “affordability” is a fake word made up by Democrats.

To no one’s surprise, his handpicked head of the Federal Reserve Board, Kevin Warsh, raised interest rates, bringing a dose of the treatment for a malady that Trump claims is fake — unacceptably high inflation.

The stock market took a huge hit as an immediate result. Less immediate, but insidious nonetheless, will be the coming uptick in interest rates across the board. Everybody who borrows money will feel this one.

More concerningto me is the longer range effect of the war in Iran and the way violence has spread across the Arabian peninsula. Oil supplies and prices are bound to be affected by this extension of the fighting westward from the Strait of Hormuz into Saudi Arabia.  

Trump’s notion that “affordability” is a figment of someone’s political imagination will be exposed, along with his other delusions of adequacy — never mind grandeur — as a real and very unpleasant result of his ineptitude and disconnection from reality.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

As if we needed more verification of President Trump’s inability to control the world and make it spin to his liking, the [Federal Reserve Board just announced](https://abcnews.com/Business/federal-reserve-expected-raise-interest-rates-time-2023/story?id=136457761) that interest rates are going up. Why? Because inflation is still unacceptably high.
Trump, who [vowed](https://thehill.com/homenews/nexstar_media_wire/5441550-trump-promised-lower-grocery-prices-on-day-one-heres-what-happened/) that grocery prices would come down on “day one” of his administration and that he would get inflation under control, has been exposed as a victim of his own ineptitude.
- Despite [warning](https://abcnews.com/Business/companies-raising-prices-response-trumps-tariffs/story?id=120900637) after [warning](https://www.hks.harvard.edu/faculty-research/policy-topics/public-finance/explainer-how-do-tariffs-work-and-how-will-they) that his tariff fixation would raise prices on nearly everything that Americans buy, Trump went ahead with his plans to tariff [just about every country](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvgj61j6l08o) in sight. The result? [Tariffs drove excess inflation](https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/federal-research-confirms-trump-tariffs-100211586.html).
- Despite his promise that the war with Iran would be [over in a few weeks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZZ9DH8ECT8A), Trump found out he grabbed a tiger by its tail. Here we are, eight months into a war that looks like it has no end in sight, dealing with some of the highest energy prices ever [because of it](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/national-security/iran-war-driving-inflation-americans-cbo-report-says-rcna597978).
- Despite blaming high prices on the Biden administration, [inflation has accelerated](https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/democrats/2026/4/updated-data-inflation-gasoline-costs-continue-to-soar-under-president-trump) since Trump took office in 2025.
These facts, as you might expect, haven’t done much to bring Trump back into contact with reality. He’s still delusionally claiming that “affordability” is a [fake word](https://www.forbes.com/sites/maryroeloffs/2026/06/17/trump-says-affordability-is-fake-word-as-inflation-hits-3-year-high/) made up by Democrats.
To no one’s surprise, his handpicked head of the Federal Reserve Board, Kevin Warsh, raised interest rates, [bringing a dose](https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/just-trump-handpicked-fed-chair-181227574.html) of the treatment for a malady that Trump claims is fake — unacceptably high inflation.
The stock market [took a huge hit](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/@DJ.1) as an immediate result. Less immediate, but insidious nonetheless, will be the coming uptick in interest rates across the board. Everybody who borrows money will feel this one.
More concerningto me is the longer range effect of the war in Iran and the way [violence has spread](https://www.icis.com/explore/resources/news/2026/09/14/11233103/industry-gathers-as-blocked-oil-and-gas-lng-exports-from-middle-east-weigh-on-plans/) across the Arabian peninsula. Oil supplies and prices are bound to be affected by this extension of the fighting westward from the Strait of Hormuz into Saudi Arabia.
Trump’s notion that “affordability” is a figment of someone’s political imagination will be exposed, along with his other delusions of adequacy — never mind grandeur — as a real and very unpleasant result of his ineptitude and disconnection from reality.

item.title: Insurers race to cover AI errors
item.description:
More than 1 in 5 U.S. companies now use artificial intelligence in their daily operations, according to a recent analysis of federal data from Goldman Sachs. In theory AI offers the promise of greater productivity and profits, but even with advances in capabilities, these systems are still fundamentally unpredictable, creating new liabilities for firms that use them.


That’s where insurance typically comes in. But AI is disrupting that business, too. Deloitte projects insurance for AI will grow into a nearly $5 billion global business by 2032.
item.source:markdown:
More than 1 in 5 U.S. companies now use artificial intelligence in their daily operations, according to **[a recent analysis](https://www.marketwatch.com/story/one-in-five-u-s-companies-is-now-using-ai-but-the-impact-on-the-job-market-remains-narrow-say-goldman-analysts-e1c7e11e)** of federal data from Goldman Sachs. In theory AI offers the promise of greater productivity and profits, but even with advances in capabilities, these systems are still fundamentally unpredictable, creating new liabilities for firms that use them.
That’s where insurance typically comes in. But AI is disrupting that business, too. Deloitte **[projects](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/multimedia/videos/ai-insurance-market-potential.html)** insurance for AI will grow into a nearly $5 billion global business by 2032.

item.title: Bwak! Bwak! Rounds a no-show for debate with Brian Bengs
item.description:
There was no empty chair visible, but South Dakota Public Broadcasting made it clear that Sen. Mike Rounds had been given the opportunity to be present, and that he had also failed to offer even one alternative date for the event.

I’m fairly certain that a determination was made by at least a few in the Rounds’ office that SDPB would simply fold its tent and forget about it. Instead, the network followed through, so independent Brian Bengs had the entire hour to share who he was, what he stands for, and why he’s in the race.

Getting big money out of our political system is #1 on Bengs’ list, and it’s increasingly becoming #1 on the list of most voters. His other main three priorities are a total hiatus on Data Centers, establish term limits on lawmakers, and somehow getting out of the ‘forever’ war we’ve begun with Iran.

Moderator Jackie Hendry did a creditable job in covering the essential questions.

And Bengs did a creditable job explaining his decades in our military as a lawyer who actually specialized in the issue of war.

He did an especially good job of telling why he ran as a Democrat against John Thune in 2022. He first registered as an independent as a teenager and, except for the 13 months running against Thune, he’s been a lifelong independent. But no one else stepped forward then, so he ran. He noted that South Dakotans in general simply refuse to vote for a Democrat, yet with the same arguments as then, he’s finding SD voters much more amenable to an independent.

You may have seen the PAC ads blasting Bengs for having run as a Democrat, as if he’s trying to fool us now with his independent status. I’m still waiting for just one Rounds ad that talks about anything that he’s accomplished. Anything. Just one.

Bengs was especially titillating when he talked about three other independent Senate candidates, all of whom are doing well and running strong campaigns.

When Hendry asked him who he’d caucus with in D. C., Bengs suggested that if all of them win, they would be their own caucus and actually control many of the upcoming votes. And he’s discussed this with those other independents.

There’s a new idea!

God knows we need new and fresh ideas.

After watching the entire hour with Brian Bengs, my wife and I agreed that we would donate to his campaign. He definitely has our vote.

We’re still waiting for that positive Rounds ad.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years.

item.title: AI safety requires action, not promises
item.description:
AI leaders suddenly seem to agree on slowing down the AI race. Anthropic's Dario Amodei published an essay last weekend calling to "pace the frontier" — slow the development of advanced AI to allow safety measures to catch up. He said Anthropic will give access to independent safety evaluators, to which OpenAI's Sam Altman and XAI's Elon Musk concurred.


It's all giving déjà vu to Amy Webb, founder of the Future Today Strategy Group, who’s been pushing government leaders around the globe to adopt a similar framework for AI for almost a decade. She laid out her vision in her 2019 book “The Big Nine: How the Tech Titans and Their Thinking Machines Could Warp Humanity.”


More on this:


“AI CEOs want to ‘pace’ the industry. That may not mean slowing down.” from NBC News


“AI's leaders just asked to slow down. I made that case nine years ago.” from Amy Webb


“We Must Pace the Frontier” from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

item.title: NHTSA orders Tesla to prove its Cybercab is legal to sell, under oath
item.description:

The agency issued a formal Special Order on September 10 demanding that the company show, under oath, how a vehicle with no steering wheel, no pedals, and no mirrors complies with federal safety standards written for human drivers.

Tesla has until September 30 to respond. Failing to answer fully and truthfully carries penalties of up to $139 million.

item.title: The world’s largest EV company just partnered with an African electric motorcycle company
item.description:
Africa’s electric motorcycle market is about to get an interesting new combination of Chinese manufacturing scale and homegrown battery-swapping infrastructure.

Yadea, the Chinese electric two-wheeler giant that has sold more than 100 million vehicles globally, has announced a new strategic partnership with African electric mobility company Spiro. The two companies plan to work together on electric motorcycles and scooters specifically tailored to African markets while integrating those vehicles into Spiro’s rapidly growing battery-swapping network.

item.title: Why a 10-year bond at a 5% yield is a pretty big deal
item.description:

This morning, we have more on why bond yields are rising and how they could affect you. item.title: Tesla’s record month: 4 fatal Autopilot and Full Self-Driving crashes
item.description:
July 2026 was the worst month on record for Tesla driver-assist crashes. Tesla reported 236 of them to federal regulators, the most it has ever filed in a single month.

Four of those crashes killed someone. In every one, Tesla’s own data says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, and in every one, the public was never told the system was involved. This is the latest from our ongoing investigation matching Tesla’s redacted NHTSA reports to real, named crashes.

item.title: Why AI models are obsessed with creatures
item.description:
The problem of AI alignment has become a hot topic. It’s raised questions, like how do we get AI to do what we want, and not what we don't want? For example, hacking another company. Or, in a less criminal vein, how do we get AI to stop talking about goblins?


After mounting user reports of this behavior earlier this year, OpenAI had to give its models — ChatGPT and Codex — explicit instructions to cut it out. It's the topic of today's “Uncanny AI,” those moments when it's clear AI doesn't think like us.


Janelle Shane, author of the blog "AI Weirdness,” says goblin mode emerged from a nerdy personality customization. “Marketplace Tech” host Meghan McCarty Carino asked her why.

item.title: How Fed interest rate increases could raise your household debt
item.description:
For most of my career I've heard predictions that the federal debt would end in collapse. The warnings have come from both parties, usually from whichever one is not in power. Not having seen a collapse yet, I'm skeptical of new warnings.

A recent one comes in a report by Ambrose Evans-Pritchard published August 11, 2026, in the Telegraph titled "The pieces are falling into place for a US financial crisis." I'm not persuaded by the forecast. But the report includes one fact that isn't a prediction at all, and it applies to your household as much as to the Treasury.

The federal government has been borrowing short. About 85% of government borrowing in recent years has been Treasury bills that mature in a year or less, which now make up 22 percent of outstanding marketable federal debt. This is higher than the range of 15 to 20 percent recommended by the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee. Roughly 20 percent of all federal debt comes due within four months.

Both parties built this. The Treasury began leaning on short-term bills in 2023, after Congress suspended the debt ceiling, and Secretary Scott Bessent continued the practice after taking office in 2025, though he had criticized it before he had the job.

The reward of this strategy is short-term savings. Net interest on the national debt is projected at $1.0 trillion in fiscal 2026, according to the Congressional Budget Office. That is more than the government spends on any other budget category except Social Security, including national defense and Medicare. Borrowing short holds that figure down. The risk is that if interest rates rise, a significant chunk of the federal debt gets refinanced at the new higher rate within twelve months.

A rate increase is a real possibility. In July the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.50 to 3.75 percent, but three regional Federal Reserve bank presidents dissented and wanted an increase. Inflation has run above the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target for more than five years.

How might a rate increase affect your own household debts? A home equity line of credit averages about 7.4 percent and adjusts with the prime rate. Credit card rates average around 20 percent and adjust the same way. Adjustable-rate mortgages reset on a set schedule. Each of those payments can change without you doing anything.

What can you do? I strongly suggest avoiding either of two extreme reactions. One is to dismiss the warning because the last several warnings were wrong. The second is to panic and rush into dramatic action that feels like taking control: selling out of stocks, buying gold, or draining savings to pay off a low fixed-rate mortgage.

A good first step instead is a debt inventory. The real risk is in a variable-interest debt you’ve come to regard as fixed. So list every debt you carry. Mark each one fixed or variable. Add up the variable balances, then recalculate those payments at three percentage points above today's rate. If your budget could absorb the new total, you may not need to do anything. If it could not, you have a specific problem with specific possible solutions: refinance the variable debt to a fixed rate, pay down the variable balances ahead of the fixed ones, or build cash reserves against the reset.

I've written before about why the federal debt may be less dire than the headlines suggest, and I still think much of that argument holds. You cannot know whether a national crisis is coming.

You can, however, assess the risk of a crisis for your own budget and take action to reduce that risk.

item.title: Bengs needs to stress issues as campaigns hit the home stretch
item.description:
I got an email from Brian Bengs this afternoon. That's not too surprising. Bengs sends me at least two emails every day, generally asking for money.

He has pointed out that his independent candidacy for U.S. Senate has a much better chance of success now that it's a two way race between him and Mike Rounds.

The Democratic candidate, Julian Beaudion, dropped out of the race at the last possible minute. Neither Bengs nor Beaudion is from South Dakota, but Beaudion has lived here longer than Bengs. Rounds didn't have much to worry about when his opposition was divided between two obscure opponents.

Recent emails from Bengs cite various polls which show that he and Rounds are statistically tied. In his emails, he sometimes he talks about fixing a morning cup of coffee, and the fact that he's living in a camper while he builds himself a house. He will remind us that he worked briefly as a park ranger at Wind Cave National Park, and that he had a career in the military before he taught briefly at Northern State University. Many national park rangers saw their jobs evaporate during Elon Musk's DOGE crusade against federal employees. 

Bengs was actually the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate back in 2022, shortly after he came to South Dakota, and he lost to John Thune by a margin of 69% to 26%. That was Joe Biden's midterm election, shortly after the Covid pandemic. Bengs switched his own voter registration back to independent just weeks after losing that election. 

His most persistent argument against giving Rounds a third term in the Senate is that Rounds is a career politician. He served in the State Senate, eventually being selected as majority leader, and then was elected Governor twice before winning a complicated race for the Senate in 2014. It's true that Mike Rounds has held public office for more than three decades, but that's not my issue with him.

Tim Johnson was a career politician, and I was proud to vote for him every time he was on the ballot. Johnson was the only South Dakotan to serve in all four legislative capacities: State Representative, State Senator, U.S. Representative and U.S. Senator. He never lost an election. Johnson wasn't flashy, but had the persona of an Eagle Scout, or even the boy next door. I usually agreed with his positions on issues, and respected his integrity. Interestingly, Tim Johnson managed to defeat John Thune, by a very narrow margin, back in 2002. 

In the fifty days remaining before this year's election, Brian Bengs could tell us where he stands on some of the hot button issues that face our state and nation.

  • Congress is years behind schedule in passing a farm bill. What would Bengs do, to break that impasse?

  • Since he worked as a park ranger, how does he feel about the Trump administration's ongoing efforts to dismantle our conservation legacy.

  • Big Bend is seriously threatened by the idiotic and destructive border wall.

  • Trump wants to sell off a chunk of Yosemite to a developer.

  • The Senate voted, 50-49, to allow an open pit copper mine right next to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area, which is America's most visited wilderness. If Rounds had found the courage to oppose that scheme, the outcome would have been different.

  • Bengs could also tell us what he proposes to do, if anything, to make housing more affordable.

  • As a military man, he could tell us what he thinks about Trump's unhinged war against Iran.

  • And he could tell us how he proposes to keep Social Security solvent. 

There are many valid reasons for South Dakotans to bring Mike Rounds' Senate tenure to an end. Rather than continually attacking him as a career politician, Bengs could take a stand on some of the issues that threaten our future as a democracy and as a nation.

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

item.title: I’m voting no on constitutional amendment L. It’s undemocratic
item.description:
John’s note: During the next few weeks I’ll be reviewing the constitutional amendments that will be coming up for a vote in November and casting my vote on them publicly, here on The Standard, before I do it for real on election day.

Constitutional Amendment L will be on South Dakota’s ballot in November. The measure is about changing the size of the majority needed for passage of constitutional amendments. 

A "yes" vote supports requiring a 60% supermajority by voters to approve constitutional amendments. 

A "no" vote opposes raising the vote threshold, maintaining a simple majority vote requirement for approving constitutional amendments.

I’l be voting no. A basic principle of democracy is that the majority rules. The concept is plain and simple enough and I don’t understand why supporters of an amendment like this insist that a minority can rule when it comes to certain questions being put to a vote. 

I think it’s ridiculous that a measure supported by 59.9% of voters can be struck down because 40.1% of the voters don’t like it. In other words, just over 40% of us can impose their will on the other nearly 60%.

That’s minority rule and it goes against the grain of how democracies are supposed to function.

I hope you’ll join me in voting no on this inherently undemocratic measure.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.title: Inflation trumps wage gains
item.description:
The latest BLS data put real hourly wage gains at -0.3% last month, compared to last year. That’s thanks to inflation running hotter than pay raises. To make up for it, some workers are putting in extra hours or dipping into their savings. In this episode, how much longer can Americans cope with what are effectively inflation-driven pay cuts? Plus: The gender wage gap slows economic productivity, housing starts grow in the Northeast as they fall elsewhere, and we weigh the possible outcomes of next week’s FOMC meeting.

item.title: Trump’s $1.2 trillion election dividend is desperate and dangerous
item.description:
President Trump is at it again, making big time promises without thinking through their ramifications. At the Republican convention that just concluded in Dallas, Trump said that every adult U.S. citizen would collect a cool five thousand bucks if Republicans hold both chambers of Congress.

The announcement is astounding, audacious and altogether crazy.

For one thing, I wonder if at some point in the lead-up to his promise Trump and his gang of sycophants actually took out a calculator and figured how much it would cost.   

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget did just that and came up with $1.2 trillion,which is about 3.5% of our country’s GDP. 

That’s just plain crazy. CRFB notes that “this proposal is fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious.”

That’s putting it mildly compared to my take, which is so crowded with expletives that I can’t, in deference to good taste, post them here.

More to the civilized  point is the fact that Trump has already promised dividends that he has yet to pay out. The guy’s a welsher.

  • Tariff dividends that he promised last year have yet to be paid.

  • DOGE dividends from cash saved by the budget cutting frenzy early on in his administration haven’t materialized.

  • Dividends are supposed to accrue from expiring ACA subsidies. Though still in its larval stage, I’m dubious about this promise, considering his track record.

Given the huge hole in our federal budget, it’s hard to see how any of those dividends will ever get paid. I wonder if anybody listening to Trump’s attempt at election bribery actually believes he'll come across this time.

The fiscal damage that the payout would cause is hard to overstate. I haven’t found a supportive economist to weigh in on this looney-tunes proposal. All I’ve found are harsh critiques.

Those critiques focus on the fiscal madness of further increasing our national debt and the inflation that would result from the $1.2 trillion that would suddenly be injected into our economy.

Trump’s promise isn’t just dangerous demagoguery. It’s irrational and illusional.  

The GOP hasn’t got much to brag about on the policy front. If it has to resort to bribery as a means of propping up support, Republicans are in sad shape.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

At the Republican convention that just concluded in Dallas, [Trump said](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/10/trump-5000-election-dividend.html) that every adult U.S. citizen would collect a cool five thousand bucks if Republicans hold both chambers of Congress.
The announcement is astounding, audacious and altogether crazy.
For one thing, I wonder if at some point in the lead-up to his promise Trump and his [gang of sycophants](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2025/aug/25/trump-staff-incompetent-sycophants) actually took out a calculator and figured how much it would cost.
The [Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget](https://www.crfb.org/press-releases/election-dividends-would-explode-deficit-and-worsen-inflation) did just that and came up with $1.2 trillion,which is about 3.5% of our country’s GDP.
That’s just plain crazy. CRFB notes that “this proposal is fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious.”
That’s putting it mildly compared to my take, which is so crowded with expletives that I can’t, in deference to good taste, post them here.
More to the civilized point is the fact that Trump has [already promised dividends](https://www.newsweek.com/every-dividend-check-donald-trump-promised-then-what-happened-next-12427685) that he has yet to pay out. The guy’s a welsher.
- Tariff dividends that he promised last year have yet to be paid.
- DOGE dividends from cash saved by the budget cutting frenzy early on in his administration haven’t materialized.
- Dividends are supposed to accrue from expiring ACA subsidies. Though still in its larval stage, I’m dubious about this promise, considering his track record.
Given the [huge hole](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/61984) in our federal budget, it’s hard to see how any of those dividends will ever get paid. I wonder if anybody listening to Trump’s attempt at election bribery actually believes he'll come across this time.
The fiscal damage that the payout would cause is hard to overstate. I haven’t found a supportive economist to weigh in on this looney-tunes proposal. All I’ve found are [harsh critiques](https://fortune.com/2026/09/10/trump-5000-dividend-national-debt-kent-smetters/).
Those critiques focus on the fiscal madness of [further increasing our national debt](https://fortune.com/2026/09/10/trump-5000-dividend-national-debt-kent-smetters/) and [the inflation](https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/personal-finance/2026/09/10/trump-5000-dividends-checks-inflation-interest-rates-economy/91690821007/) that would result from the $1.2 trillion that would suddenly be injected into our economy.
Trump’s promise isn’t just dangerous demagoguery. It’s irrational and illusional.
The GOP hasn’t got much to brag about on the policy front. If it has to resort to bribery as a means of propping up support, Republicans are in sad shape.

item.title: AI safety concerns grow as insiders issue urgent warnings
item.description:
An Anthropic researcher publicly resigned this week, warning on social media that artificial intelligence companies are “gambling with our lives.”


It’s part of a growing chorus of insiders pleading to slow down the AI race. One said he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the tech will kill us all in the next decade.


The news comes after a fresh wave of troubling details about the OpenAI incident where agents escaped a testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face.


Plus, data center developers have their eye on Patagonia — the colder, the better. And Amazon is betting AI lip-syncing can make dubbed video content more watchable.


Maria Curi, tech policy reporter at Axios, joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino to break down the busy week in tech news.


Everything we talked about:


Scoop: Sanders convenes senators for AI briefing amid mounting alarm — from Axios


Tech explores Argentina's Patagonia for mega data centers — from Reuters


Google to invest record $15 billion in AI infrastructure in the ‘Texas of Europe’ — from CNBC


Amazon Prime Video’s new AI tech matches lips to dubbed audio — from The Verge

The news comes after a fresh wave of troubling details about the [OpenAI incident](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/openai-hugging-face-hack-ai-risks/) where agents escaped a testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face.
Plus, data center developers have their eye on Patagonia — the colder, the better. And Amazon is betting AI lip-syncing can make dubbed video content more watchable.
Maria Curi, tech policy reporter at Axios, joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino to break down the busy week in tech news.

item.title: Tesla Autopilot was on in I-35 crash that killed its driver
item.description:
A 2024 Tesla Model Y ran off Interstate 35 in rural Missouri, struck a guardrail, and killed its driver, a 64-year-old woman from Raymore. Troopers reported a single-vehicle wreck and said the car “went off the road.”

What they didn’t say, and likely didn’t know, is that Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says the car’s driver-assist system was engaged. This is part of an ongoing Electrek investigation matching reported crashes to Tesla’s redacted NHTSA data.

more…
item.source:markdown:
![](https://electrek.co/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2020/10/Tesla-Autopilot-Radar-e1603395743425.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1200)
A 2024 Tesla Model Y ran off Interstate 35 in rural Missouri, struck a guardrail, and killed its driver, a 64-year-old woman from Raymore. Troopers reported a single-vehicle wreck and said the car “went off the road.”
What they didn’t say, and likely didn’t know, is that Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says the car’s driver-assist system was engaged. This is part of an [ongoing Electrek investigation](https://electrek.co/2026/09/01/tesla-autopilot-fsd-crashes-hidden-data/) matching reported crashes to Tesla’s redacted NHTSA data.

item.title: What's so concerning about the Hugging Face hack?
item.description:
Nate Soares has been worried about artificial intelligence longer than almost anyone.


He's the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and co-author of the subtly named book, "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All."


He's watched with a sort of grim vindication, as increasingly alarming details emerge about the hack of the AI company Hugging Face by OpenAI models in development.


OpenAI and third-party investigators recently released reports outlining what went wrong. Soares worries it's not enough.


More on this:


The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead - From OpenAI


Brief independent investigation of agents’ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident - From METR and Redwood Research
item.source:markdown:
Nate Soares has been worried about artificial intelligence longer than almost anyone.
He's the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and co-author of the subtly named book, " [If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/eliezer-yudkowsky/if-anyone-builds-it-everyone-dies/9780316595643/)."
He's watched with a sort of grim vindication, as increasingly alarming details emerge about the hack of the AI company Hugging Face by OpenAI models in development.
OpenAI and third-party investigators recently released reports outlining what went wrong. Soares worries it's not enough.

item.title: How financial advisors for couples can get the “silent partner” involved
item.description:
Over 40-plus years in financial planning, I noticed a common pattern with client couples: in meetings with advisors, one partner usually does most of the talking. The other sits back, nods in the right places, and answers direct questions. The professionals in the room key off the partner who talks. That's a natural response. It’s efficient. It also helps keep one spouse ignorant around the family finances.

How can planners help change the “silent partner” dynamic? I learned the value of actively bringing the quieter partner into the conversation by turning toward them, making eye contact, and asking for their thoughts. Even if the answer is still a shrug, the question signals that their view belongs in the conversation.

It also helps to suspend judgment and gently explore why someone is reluctant to participate. They may feel less “qualified” if they earn less than their partner. They may be afraid of looking foolish in front of two people who understand something they do not.

Many couples divide up the money work. Most of the time it doesn’t matter who manages the bills, tracks account balances, or does the tax returns. The arrangement turns risky when one partner doesn’t know enough about the finances. That lack of involvement can have serious consequences.

One concern is that eventually one partner will almost certainly need to handle the money alone as a result of death, divorce, or incapacity. I have sat with surviving spouses needing to learn everything about their finances at the worst possible moment. A few could not even name the bank that held their checking account.

Sometimes a partner is shut out on purpose. The National Network to End Domestic Violence reports that financial abuse occurs in 99 percent of domestic violence cases. For an abuser, keeping a partner ignorant about family finances is a way to control them and limit their options.

For planners, disregarding a silent partner also raises a question of ethics. A planner in a financial therapy study group I take part in described one client couple who were spending past their income and carrying a burden of debt. The husband handled their finances, knew how bad things were, and was communicating with the planner. The wife didn’t come to meetings, appeared to have no idea, and kept on spending. The planner realized she had become complicit in a destructive pattern of secret-keeping.

Joy Slabaugh, a Certified Financial Planner™ and licensed therapist who taught advisors to recognize financial abuse at this year's Financial Planning Association NorCal conference, offers a practical approach. Couple counselors commonly work under a stated policy that they will not hold a secret from one partner on behalf of the other. She recommends that planners do something similar, writing into the client agreement that they will meet individually with each partner on a set schedule.

Her recommendation was new to me, and it makes sense. It helps advisors maintain their clarity about representing both partners. It gives a partner who is used to staying in the background a chance to be heard without having to initiate a separate meeting. Also, if either partner strongly opposes the idea, that reaction is important information.

I have written before about the qualities to look for in an advisor who works well with couples. It would be worthwhile to also ask whether the firm will meet with each of you separately. One solo conversation a year would help give the silent partner a voice. It would help both the couple and the advisor to remember that, no matter who handles the accounts or earns the most money, the partners are equals in the financial planning relationship.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

Plus: Rising oil prices push up short-term bond yields, more homebuyers look into adjustable-rate mortgages, and we try to predict Fed Chair Warsh’s next move.

item.title: Where housing and childcare eat up the most income

Paying for housing and childcare can eat up more than half of the median U.S. family’s income, a new report finds. The least affordable metro areas in the country for working families with kids are Los Angeles and New York City, where the median cost of childcare plus the notoriously high cost of housing devour 95% or more of the median income. item.title: Data confirms Autopilot/FSD was active in crash that killed a mother, passerby saved her baby
item.description:
A 2021 Tesla Model Y left an Alabama highway, hit two trees, and caught fire, killing its driver, 29-year-old Kayleigh Page. Her 7-month-old daughter was pulled from the burning car by a stranger who saw it happen.

Troopers reported it as a single-vehicle wreck. What they didn’t say, and likely didn’t know, is that Tesla’s own data shows the car’s driver-assist system was engaged. This is part of an ongoing Electrek investigation matching reported crashes to Tesla’s redacted NHTSA data.

item.title: Let SNAP users buy what they want. We don’t need a nanny state
item.description:
Cory Heidelberger just posted a piece in Dakota Free Press about how South Dakota retailers are uneasy about this year’s implementation of a bill that would deny sales of soft drinks to SNAP users in our grocery stores. SNAP stands for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, once familiarly known as “food stamps.”

Denying SNAP users access to soft drinks in the name of improving diets lends itself to a collectively smug sense of noblesse oblige, but it incurs some practical challenges for the food industry, particularly if the trend toward eliminating “junk food” from a SNAP purchaser's grocery cart spilled over (as it has in Texas, where the photo above was taken) to other products in South Dakota.

On the retail front, the new regulation is likely to cause some confusion in grocery stores throughout our state. Heidelberger’s piece notes that its implementation will create some administrative chaos, both within the private and public sectors as retailers and civil authorities debate and classify which products are or are not soft drinks. 

On a broader scale, if food purchases are further restricted, retailers will have a long list of issues that they’ll have to deal with. First off, how do we come to a common definition of “junk food?” The concept is subjective and vague. I haven’t been able to find a universally recognized, scientifically based definition.

More difficult to quantify are the social effects of telling people how to spend the money they get from the state. Free choice is perhaps the essence of a democratic society. Does singling out a particular class of residents and denying them free choice at the food store extend the liberties that we cherish as Americans?  Of course not.  It stigmatizes and alienates people who have been taught early on that their access to some food items is restricted.

Think about kids from poor families who are old enough to figure out what’s going on. While grocery shopping with their families, a sign like the one above cuts them off from the aisle where all the treats are. Their more well-off schoolmates can buy that stuff at will, but they can’t. Could there be a more painful sense of exclusion?

Food choice restrictions based on income are an affront to human dignity and may do more harm than good. 

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.    

Photo: public domain, wikimedia commons

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

Their more well-off schoolmates can buy that stuff at will, but they can’t. Could there be a more painful sense of exclusion?

item.title: Meta's youth safety settlement could change how people access the internet
item.description:
Meta agreed to a settlement last month with 52 attorneys general in a landmark case over teen social media addiction. The company promised a number of restrictions for under 18-year-old users, like time limits, overnight blackouts on some features and hidden likes. It also agreed to pay up to $17 billion, partly contingent on TikTok and YouTube adopting similar reforms.


Surveys show a strong majority of Americans support stricter limitations on social media for kids. But, this settlement could fundamentally change how everyone accesses the internet, according to Will Creeley, legal director at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression.


More on this:


“That $17B Meta settlement comes with a catch: Your online speech rights” from The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression


“Majority of Americans support banning social media for kids under 16” from Pew Research Center

item.title: Tesla Cybercab has a hidden virtual joystick to drive it manually
item.description:
A Tesla Cybercab rider found something in the robotaxi: a manual driving mode. When he got in, the touchscreen was showing a virtual joystick to drive the car by hand.

Tesla built the Cybercab with no steering wheel and no pedals. But it apparently still has a way to drive it manually, and you do it by dragging a finger across a screen.
